claims.text: Adding 5–10 vol% MoS2 to CoCrFeNi will reduce friction from room temperature to 800 °C.
Adding 5–10 vol% MoS2 to CoCrFeNi will reduce wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C.
The incorporated MoS2 will form a lubricating tribofilm on the sliding surface.
The tribofilm will contain MoS2 and high-temperature decomposition products of MoS2.
At low temperatures, layered MoS2 reduces friction through easy interlayer shear.
At elevated temperatures, MoS2 decomposes to form oxides such as MoO3.
MoO3 formed at elevated temperature is lubricious.
The MoS2-derived tribofilm reduces adhesive and abrasive interactions.
The MoS2-derived tribofilm adapts to variations in temperature and load.
The modified composite will have a coefficient of friction below 0.3 throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The modified composite will have a wear rate below 10^-6 mm^3/Nm throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The modified composite will have lower friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi under loads of 5–20 N in both ambient air and inert gas.
The modified composite will have lower wear than unmodified CoCrFeNi under loads of 5–20 N in both ambient air and inert gas.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi is expected to exhibit higher friction and wear, particularly at elevated temperatures.
The proposed performance may not persist in vacuum or highly reactive environments because MoS2 decomposition products may be unstable.
MoS2-derived lubrication at 800 °C may be limited by instability of its decomposition products.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis applies the elevated-temperature MoO3-based mechanism to both ambient air and inert gas, but it does not explain how substantial oxide formation would occur or remain equivalent in an inert environment.
